analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it with new taxes on income above $250,000 and on investment gains.
analysis.headline: The Social Security Expansion Act was introduced in the Senate with 11 backers, all from the Democratic caucus, and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced; it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would increase Social Security checks for current and future retirees, use a more accurate inflation index for seniors, set a higher minimum benefit so lifetime low earners reach at least the poverty line, and let children of deceased or disabled workers keep benefits through college until age 22. To pay for it, it would apply the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $250,000 (today wages above the cap are untaxed) and sharply raise the tax on investment income, from 3.8% to 16.2%. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries and their families: every retiree and disabled worker would get a roughly 5% boost in the benefit formula, annual cost-of-living adjustments would track the spending patterns of people over 62, lifetime low earners would get a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line that grows with each year worked, and college students who lost a disabled or deceased parent could collect benefits until 22.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, low earners, students

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first benefit formula tier from 90% to 95% of earnings and lifts a key dollar threshold by 18%, increasing benefits for current and future beneficiaries.
Switches the cost-of-living formula to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the prices seniors actually pay.
Creates a new minimum benefit for long-worked, low-paid careers, scaled up to 125% of the poverty guideline for workers with 30 or more years of work.
Lets children of deceased or disabled workers who are full-time students collect benefits until age 22, up from 19 for post-secondary students.

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to earnings between the current cap ($176,100 in 2025) and $250,000, and indefinitely to earnings above $250,000, and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% while extending it to active business income.
Merges the retirement and disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Households with wage or self-employment income above $250,000 would pay Social Security tax on all of it, and households with large investment income or active business profits would pay a much higher tax on those gains — costs concentrated at the top of the income distribution.

drawbacks.text: The tax increase is steep: the investment income tax rises more than fourfold, from 3.8% to 16.2%, and extends to active business income, which means owners of profitable pass-through businesses face a much larger tax bill; critics argue this could reduce business investment and hiring.
The new minimum benefit requires at least 10 years of covered work, so people with very short working careers get less help than the poverty-line framing suggests.
The benefit increases are permanent commitments, so if the new taxes underperform projections, Congress would face pressure to cut benefits or raise taxes again.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on households above $250,000 in wage income and on large investment gains, while the benefits go to a program serving tens of millions of retirees, disabled workers, and their families. The main honest risk is actuarial: benefit formulas are locked in permanently while tax revenue depends on forecasts. On its own terms — higher benefits, solvency, funded by the top of the income distribution — the design is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2025 by Senator Sanders with 10 Democratic cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high earners and holders of large investment income keep the current tax cap, since nothing has moved. Retirees and low earners get nothing yet, but the bill can still act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and big investors, so far

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 27, 2025.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren, Edward Markey, Jeff Merkley, Peter Welch, Alex Padilla, Tina Smith, Chris Van Hollen, Cory Booker, Kirsten Gillibrand, Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for Social Security and tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has taken no action on it since February 27, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors caucus with Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing Finance, the bill has not moved.

industries.note: The tax on investment gains would jump from 3.8% to 16.2% and now cover active business profits, so affluent households would pay substantially more; ordinary beneficiaries would receive the revenue as higher benefits.

The Social Security payroll tax, currently capped at $176,100 of wages, would apply to all earnings above $250,000, including self-employment income for owners of professional practices and small businesses.
A much higher tax on investment gains would modestly discourage some portfolio activity and could shift how fund managers structure income, though the direct cost falls on their high-income clients.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans controlling the Senate and chairing the Finance Committee, a tax-and-benefits bill with no Republican cosponsors is very unlikely to get a hearing or a markup this Congress; the most common path for a bill in this position is to expire at the end of the session without a vote, though its provisions can resurface in future Congresses.
